subject: technology
unit_title: Secure Data Project and Threat-Model Review
essential_question: How do we build something that holds data responsibly and can prove it?
standards: Michigan Computer Science: Data and Analysis
project_brief: Deliver a secure data application with schema, tests, a threat model, mitigations, and a privacy impact review. This is the grade 10 culminating project for "Secure Data Project and Threat-Model Review" (ma-g10-technology-u06, unit 6), built around requirements and data inventory, structure and query implementation, validation and error handling, threat model and mitigations, and privacy impact and minimization. Collect or use a small, fictional or already-approved data set related to requirements and data inventory, structure and query implementation, validation and error handling, and threat model and mitigations, and turn it into a labeled visual with a one-paragraph, evidence-based conclusion.
requirements: Address every topic listed for this unit: requirements and data inventory, structure and query implementation, validation and error handling, threat model and mitigations, privacy impact and minimization, and documentation and review.
Meet the performance task as written: Deliver a secure data application with schema, tests, a threat model, mitigations, and a privacy impact review.
Show your work or process, not just a final result — a process note, sketch log, commit history, or draft trail.
Complete the checklist in this package before submitting.
primary_task: Collect or use a small, fictional or already-approved data set related to requirements and data inventory, structure and query implementation, validation and error handling, and threat model and mitigations, and turn it into a labeled visual with a one-paragraph, evidence-based conclusion.
test_or_check_criteria: Every claim or design choice in the submission can be traced to requirements and data inventory or another named topic from this unit — nothing is left unexplained.
The submission runs, displays, or demonstrates correctly on at least two different sample inputs or scenarios the student chooses.
No real password, API key, account credential, precise location, or other real personal/system data appears anywhere in the submission — fictional or sandbox examples only.
The student can explain, in their own words, why each step or decision was made, not just that it works.

presentation_and_privacy.sandbox_and_credentials_note: This project never touches a real account, a real password or API key, a live production system, or another person's real data. Use fictional names, sandbox environments, local files, or already-approved sample data throughout. Submit code, screenshots of your own sandbox, diagrams, or a written walkthrough — a live public deployment is never required.

copyright_and_authorship: The final submitted work must remain your own authorship. A parent, tutor, or AI assistant may help you plan, explain a concept, demonstrate a technique, or give feedback on a draft, but may not produce the graded work itself. Never request, store, or submit a real password, API key, access token, or other real credential; use only fictional accounts and sandboxed or offline systems.
remediation: If the project stalls, step back to the smallest version of the task: rebuild just the part covering requirements and data inventory in isolation, using a worked example from this unit as a model, then re-attach it to the full project once that smaller piece works and you can explain why.
extension: Once the core project is working, extend it to handle a new constraint or edge case related to structure and query implementation, or compare two different approaches to the same problem and explain the real tradeoff between them in your own words.
